title: Linked List
html:
Linked List

Nodes holding a value and a reference onward. Worth understanding less because you will build one and more because the pointer manipulation it forces is the same manipulation trees and graphs need.

What it costs

Operation Linked list Array
Index access O(n) O(1)
Insert/remove at a known node O(1) O(n)
Insert/remove at front O(1) O(n)
Append O(1) with a tail pointer O(1) amortised
Memory per element value + pointer value
Cache behaviour poor - nodes scattered good - contiguous

The O(1) insert is the selling point and it comes with a catch: it is O(1) once you are holding the node. Getting there is O(n). A list is a good choice when you already have the position - an LRU cache moving a node to the front, a queue with head and tail pointers - and a poor one when you are indexing.

In practice, an array-backed list wins far more often than the complexity table suggests, because contiguity means each cache line fetch brings several elements while a node walk pays a miss per node.

The techniques

Dummy head. Allocate a throwaway node in front of the real head. Every insert and delete then has a predecessor, so the "what if it is the first element" branch disappears. Return dummy.next at the end. This one habit removes most linked-list bugs.

Two pointers at different speeds. One advances by one, the other by two. The fast one reaches the end when the slow one is at the middle - that is how you find a midpoint in one pass. If a cycle exists they meet inside it, because the gap between them changes by exactly one per step.

Reversal. Three pointers - previous, current, next - walking forward and flipping each link. Save next before overwriting current.next, or you lose the rest of the list. Worth writing from memory until it is automatic; reversing a sublist, testing a palindrome, and reordering all reduce to it.

Merging. Two sorted lists become one by repeatedly taking the smaller head. With a dummy head this is a dozen lines and no special cases.

Where it appears for real

Rarely as a bare structure. It appears inside things: hash table collision chains, the intrusive lists an allocator keeps of free blocks, an LRU cache's recency order paired with a map for O(1) lookup. That last combination is the canonical example of two structures covering each other's weakness - the map gives lookup, the list gives ordering, and each node is in both.

Common mistakes

  • Losing the remainder of the list by reassigning a next before saving it.
  • Forgetting to update the tail pointer, so appends silently vanish.
  • Not handling the empty list and the single-node list; almost every bug lives in one of those two.
  • Building a cycle by accident and turning a traversal into an infinite loop.
